== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:
   - If `Retrieval status` is `not_accessible` (or the paper text below says `[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE]`), you MUST set `paper_read = "not accessible"`, `study_design_identified = "cannot_tell (full text not accessible)"`, `chosen_tool = "cannot_tell"`, `why_tool_chosen = "full text not accessible"`, `overall_rating = "cannot_tell"`, `domain_ratings = []`, all 7 `cross_tool_domains` fields to `"cannot_tell"`, `overall_narrative_summary = "Full text not accessible; no risk-of-bias appraisal performed."`, `where_found_summary = "not accessible"`, and `evidence_quotes = []`. NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concerns: Cluster/village retention at 3.6 years was very high (329 of 332 randomized villages assessed; 99.1%), and 86% of 5-month respondents (1,133/1,312; 88% of households) were re-interviewed at 3.6 years, but 140 longitudinal households (11%) were replaced, 2,142 of 2,374 eligible households (90.2%) contributed valid child length-for-age Z-scores in Table 3, and the absence of pre-intervention baseline data prevents completely ruling out differential post-randomization out-migration (arm-specific flow details in Fig 1 are in an unrendered figure graphic).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Low concern: Treatment was randomly assigned at the cluster level by the research team in Stata within 12 province-by-cluster-size randomization blocks, all intention-to-treat regressions included stratum fixed effects (plus child age and sex indicators for child health outcomes), and time-invariant respondent and household characteristics at 3.6 years were well balanced across arms (Table 2), although pre-randomization baseline outcome data were not collected.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: The DRC national Healthy Villages and Schools governance intervention (seven village norms, 9-step Health Zone-community agreement, elected village WASH committee, and Community Action Plan for Maintenance) is clearly specified, and local institutional persistence was operationalized via a standardized multi-item WASH governance index (committee presence, meeting frequency, non-maintenance expenses, maintenance plan, and community health/hygiene tracking) alongside subjective governance perception items, though institutional index components relied on survey reports rather than independent administrative records.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some concerns (domain-specific divergence between objective and self-reported measures): Neither participants nor independent IHfRA enumerators were masked to treatment status. Objective protocols were used for child length-for-age Z-scores (supervisor duplicate checks), E. coli/thermotolerant coliform MPN testing of village water points and household storage containers, observed water point functionality, and 2-hour pre-interview structured handwashing observations, whereas primary 7-day diarrhea, the WASH institutions index, improved water/sanitation access, and water governance perceptions relied on unmasked respondent self-report (with social-desirability reactivity empirically shown by +9 pp self-reported handwashing vs null observed handwashing).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Strong for biophysical and observational WASH/health outcomes; moderate/weak for self-reported access and morbidity: Anthropometry (Salter scales and wall-mounted rods with supervisor re-measurement), microbial drinking water quality (Aquagenx Compartment Bag Test for E. coli and total coliform MPN at sources and household containers), water point functionality (direct observation), and handwashing (2-hour structured observation prior to interviews) were rigorously measured, whereas primary 7-day child diarrhea and household use of JMP-defined improved water and sanitation facilities relied on unmasked self-reports.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concerns: The trial was not prospectively registered prior to the March-June 2018 cluster randomization because no baseline data were collected; initial AEA registration occurred in late 2019 (5-month wave), PACTR registration in February 2021, and the 3.6-year follow-up outcome update and pre-analysis plan were posted in April 2023 at the conclusion of 3.6-year fieldwork (November 2022-February/April 2023), though the authors attest that principal investigators had not seen the 3.6-year data prior to posting and transparently report null primary health results with open microdata and code.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concerns: Computerized block randomization of 121 village clusters (339 eligible villages) in Stata was appropriate, but 7 villages were dropped post-randomization (6 randomly to meet operational targets and 1 control village due to a coding error), no baseline survey was conducted before randomization, and all participating households were sampled and recruited post-intervention in unmasked clusters (substantially mitigated by random-walk nth-household selection and restricting eligibility to residents living in the village for at least 4 years, i.e., prior to the intervention).

domain_ratings.justification: The research team centrally randomized 121 spatial clusters (grouped with >=2.5 km buffers, >=1 km in South Kivu) in Stata using stratified block randomization across 12 province-by-cluster-size blocks, and time-invariant household/respondent covariates at 3.6 years were well balanced across arms (Table 2). However, no baseline data were collected prior to randomization, and after randomization the investigators dropped 6 villages randomly from the largest clusters to meet operational targets plus 1 control village in Kasai due to a coding error (leaving 146 villages in 50 intervention clusters and 186 villages in 71 control clusters), warranting Some concerns.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (p. 1); Methods - Study design and participants & Randomization and masking (pp. 4-5); Results - Table 2 (p. 10); Discussion (p. 13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters
domain_ratings.justification: No individual households were enrolled prior to cluster randomization; all households were sampled and recruited after randomization and intervention implementation (4 households per village at 5 months post-intervention and 6 newly sampled households per village at 3.6 years post-intervention) by unmasked interviewers in unmasked communities, and unavailable/unwilling households were replaced. Selection bias was substantially mitigated by a standardized random-walk rule from the village center (every nth household, n randomly drawn from 1-20), restricting eligibility to residents who had lived in the village for >=4 years (prior to the intervention), and balanced demographic characteristics across arms (Table 2), resulting in Some concerns rather than High risk.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods - Study design and participants, Randomization and masking & Outcomes (pp. 5-6); Results (p. 8, Table 2 on p. 10); Discussion (p. 13)

domain_ratings.justification: Although neither participants nor implementers were masked due to the visible, participatory nature of community mobilization and infrastructure construction, the trial evaluated a government-led national WASH program implemented at scale without trial-induced co-interventions or artificial context deviations. Incomplete program adherence in the intervention arm (96% created an action plan; 86% implemented it) reflects realistic real-world implementation in rural/conflict-affected DRC, and all primary and secondary effects were appropriately analyzed by intention-to-treat according to original cluster assignment with stratum fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (pp. 1-2); Methods - Randomization and masking, Procedures & Statistical analyses (pp. 5-8); Results (p. 8); Discussion (p. 13)

domain_ratings.justification: Cluster-level retention at 3.6 years was excellent, with the primary WASH institutions index measured in 329 of 332 randomized villages (144/146 intervention [98.6%] and 185/186 control [99.5%]; Table 3) and 3,283 households interviewed overall. However, among the 1,312 respondents interviewed at 5 months, 1,133 (86%; 88% of households) were re-interviewed at 3.6 years with 140 households (11%) replaced; 2,142 of 2,374 eligible households (90.2%) had analyzed child length-for-age Z-scores in Table 3; arm-by-arm attrition counts in Fig 1 are in an unrendered image; and the lack of pre-randomization baseline data prevents definitively ruling out differential permanent out-migration, warranting Some concerns.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results (pp. 8-10, Fig 1 caption on p. 9, Table 3 on p. 10); Discussion (p. 13)

domain_ratings.justification: Data were collected using identical protocols across arms by an independent research firm (IHfRA) with real-time QC, 15% village re-interviews, supervisor anthropometry re-measurements, pre-interview 2-hour structured handwashing observations, direct observation of water point functionality, and Aquagenx Compartment Bag Test E. coli/coliform water quality testing. Thus, child length-for-age Z-score and biophysical/observational secondary outcomes had low measurement bias risk. However, neither participants nor enumerators were masked, and primary 7-day caregiver-reported diarrhea, the primary WASH governance index, self-reported improved water/sanitation access, and water governance perceptions relied on unmasked survey reports; the authors explicitly note social-desirability bias and show empirically that self-reported handwashing increased (+9 pp) while structured observation found no difference, warranting Some concerns across the trial's composite outcome set.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (pp. 1-2); Methods - Randomization and masking, Procedures & Outcomes (pp. 5-7); Results (pp. 10-12); Discussion (p. 13)

domain_ratings.justification: The trial was not registered prior to cluster randomization (March-June 2018) because no baseline survey was conducted. Initial AEA registration occurred in late 2019 (5-month follow-up) and PACTR registration in February 2021, while the 3.6-year follow-up outcome update and pre-analysis plan were posted in April 2023 after 3.6-year data collection had started and largely concluded (November 2022 to February/April 2023) during which real-time cloud QC occurred. Although the authors report that principal investigators had not inspected the 3.6-year data before posting the April 2023 PAP, adhere to pre-specified indices and subgroup tests, and share de-identified microdata and replication code publicly, retrospective registration and end-of-fieldwork PAP posting warrant Some concerns.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (pp. 1-2); Data availability statement (p. 2); Methods - Study design and participants & Statistical analyses (pp. 4, 8); Results (pp. 8, 12)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Study S294 (Quattrochi et al., 2025) is a large, policy-embedded cluster-randomized controlled trial evaluating the 3.6-year sustainability and health/institutional impacts of the DRC's national community-driven Healthy Villages WASH program across 121 spatial village clusters (332 villages; 3,283 households) in four provinces. Appraised with the RoB 2 cluster-randomized trials variant, the overall risk of bias is judged as Some concerns (with Low risk in D2 and Some concerns in D1a, D1b, D3, D4, and D5). Major methodological strengths include centralized stratified block randomization in Stata with >=2.5 km (>=1 km in South Kivu) spatial buffers to limit spillovers, intention-to-treat estimation with stratum fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors, 99.1% village retention (329/332 villages) at 3.6 years, data collection by an independent research organization (IHfRA) with 15% village re-interviews and supervisor anthropometry re-checks, public availability of microdata and replication code, and objective measurement of child linear growth, E. coli/thermotolerant coliform water quality, water point functionality, and structured pre-interview handwashing observations. Key limitations driving Some concerns are: (1) absence of a pre-randomization baseline survey and post-randomization dropping of 7 villages (6 randomly for operational targets and 1 control village due to a coding error) (D1a); (2) post-randomization, post-intervention household sampling and recruitment by unmasked enumerators, though mitigated by random-walk selection and a >=4-year residency criterion (D1b); (3) 11%-14% longitudinal household attrition/replacement and ~10% missing child LAZ among eligible households without baseline data to verify non-differential out-migration (D3); (4) unmasked self-reporting for primary diarrhea, the WASH governance index, improved water/sanitation use, and governance perceptions, where reactivity is underscored by +9 pp self-reported handwashing alongside null structured handwashing observation and null household E. coli differences (D4); and (5) retrospective trial registration with the 3.6-year pre-analysis plan posted in April 2023 at the end of fieldwork, albeit before principal investigators inspected the data (D5).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (121 geographic village clusters comprising 332 rural villages across four DRC provinces, stratified block-randomized to 50 intervention clusters and 71 control clusters, assessed at median 3.6 years post-intervention)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Design, registration timeline, spatial clustering, and household eligibility/sampling: Abstract (pp. 1-2) and Methods - Study design and participants (pp. 4-5). Block randomization, post-randomization village exclusions, and lack of masking: Methods - Randomization and masking (p. 5). Intervention norms/steps, QC checks, anthropometry, Aquagenx water testing, structured handwashing observation, and survey governance/access measures: Methods - Procedures & Outcomes and Table 1 (pp. 5-7). Power and ITT linear regression models: Methods - Statistical analyses (pp. 7-8). Sample retention, covariate balance, and treatment effect estimates: Results, Fig 1 caption, Table 2, Table 3, and Fig 2 (pp. 8-12). Study limitations (adherence, lack of baseline, migration/attrition, social-desirability bias): Discussion (p. 13).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study randomly assigned multi-village geographic clusters (121 clusters containing 332 villages) to a community-driven WASH and local institutional strengthening intervention (50 clusters) or control (71 clusters) and analyzed outcomes at village, household, and child levels. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, a cluster-randomized controlled trial requires the RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant) covering all six official domains (D1a, D1b, D2, D3, D4, D5).
